figures.title: The fat family tree: the map of this lesson

segments.name: Fats Overview
segments.text: Fat is one of the three macronutrients, alongside protein and carbohydrates, and it's the most energy-dense: every gram of fat gives about 9 calories, while protein and carbs give about 4. In your body, fat is stored energy, it builds the membranes around every cell, it helps you absorb vitamins A, D, E and K, and some fats are raw material for signaling molecules.

segments.name: Triglycerides and Chains
segments.text: Almost all the fat in food comes as triglycerides: a glycerol backbone holding three fatty acids, and each fatty acid is a chain of carbon atoms. What makes one fat different from another is those chains, specifically whether they have any double bonds between carbons.

segments.name: Three Categories
segments.text: That gives three main categories. Saturated fats have no double bonds, so the chain is straight and packed full of hydrogen; they're common in butter, beef fat and coconut oil and, because they can pack tightly together, tend to be solid at room temperature. Monounsaturated fats have exactly one double bond, and polyunsaturated fats have two or more. Those last two are the two kinds of unsaturated fat, and each double bond usually puts a kink in the chain, which is why olive oil, canola and nut oils stay liquid.

segments.name: Omega Families
segments.text: Within polyunsaturated fats there are two important families, omega-3 and omega-6, named for where the first double bond sits when you count from the tail end of the chain. Your body can't make the parent omega-3, ALA, or the parent omega-6, linoleic acid, so they're essential and have to come from food: omega-3 from flax, walnuts and oily fish, and omega-6 from seed oils, nuts and poultry.

segments.name: Trans Fats
segments.text: Finally there are trans fats. A small amount occurs naturally in dairy, beef and lamb, but most trans fat in food was man-made by partially hydrogenating unsaturated oils, which straightens the chains so the oil turns solid. Trans fat raises LDL and lowers HDL cholesterol, which is why it's now banned in the US and limited in the EU.

segments.name: The Mix
segments.text: Every fat in food is a mix of all these types; we just label it by the one that dominates.

figures.title: Fats and Oils Are the Same Thing
figures.subtitle: Same kind of molecule, different packing.

segments.name: Same Kind of Molecule
segments.text: Fats and oils are the same kind of molecule, a triglyceride, made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and the only difference is how tightly the chains pack. We'll see why in Figures 3 and 4.
segments.cue: Title and subtitle: same kind of molecule, different packing

segments.name: Fat Versus Oil
segments.text: The first image puts a fat above an oil. On top is tristearin, three straight saturated chains, which melts at about 72 °C, so it's solid. Below is triolein, three kinked chains with one cis double bond each, which melts at about 5 °C, so it's liquid. They're the same kind of molecule made of the same elements, carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; the oil just has six fewer hydrogens because of its three double bonds. So 'fat' or 'oil' only tells you whether it's solid or liquid at room temperature, about 20 to 25 °C. Real fats are mixes, too: coconut oil is mostly saturated and melts around 24 °C, so it's solid in a cool kitchen and liquid in a warm one. The next image shows why that shape matters, and trans fats, which we meet in Figure 4, are mostly man-made.
segments.cue: Top: FAT, tristearin; below: OIL, triolein; element lines

segments.name: Atoms at True Size
segments.text: The next image is in the space-filling style, with every atom drawn at its true size, so each fatty acid looks like a solid rod.

segments.name: Straight Chains Pack Tight
segments.text: On the left, four straight saturated chains stack tightly, like pencils in a box. They grip each other, so it takes more heat to melt them, about 69 °C for stearic acid, and that's why butter, lard and cocoa butter are solid at room temperature.

segments.name: Trans Packs Almost as Tight
segments.text: In the middle are trans chains, which we meet in Figure 4. They are almost straight, so they pack almost as tightly and melt at about 45 °C, which is why partially hydrogenated oil turned solid.

segments.name: Kinks Leave Gaps
segments.text: On the right, the cis kinks keep the oleic chains apart and leave gaps, so they slide past each other and melt at about 13 °C, and that's why olive and canola oil are liquid. In real fats these chains sit on triglycerides, like the two in the image above, and the same rule holds.

segments.name: What Is a Bond?
segments.text: A bond is the attraction that holds two atoms together in a molecule. In the fats we're looking at, it's mostly carbon sharing electrons with hydrogen or with another carbon, and that sharing is what builds the chains.
segments.cue: Meet the atoms, panel A: C and H share one pair of electrons (blue dots)

segments.name: How Bonds Work
segments.text: Atoms have electrons in shells around them, and atoms are happiest when their outer shell is full. A bond is when two atoms share a pair of those outer electrons so each one gets to count them. One shared pair is a single bond, which lets the atoms spin freely around each other. Two shared pairs is a double bond, which is shorter, stronger, and locks the atoms in place so they can't rotate. That's the whole trick behind saturated versus unsaturated fat: saturated chains are all single bonds, so they lie straight and pack tight. Unsaturated ones have double bonds that put a kink in the chain, and that's what keeps oils liquid.
segments.cue: Panels A to C: shared pair, single vs double bond, straight vs kinked chain

segments.name: Cis and Trans Footnote
segments.text: One footnote: the kink comes from cis double bonds; trans double bonds stay nearly straight. We'll see that in Figure 4.

segments.name: The Triglyceride
segments.text: Now the triglyceride image. Almost every fat you eat, and the fat stored in your body, is one kind of molecule called a triglyceride. The purple box on the left is the glycerol backbone, three carbons long, and hanging off it are three fatty acids. Each fatty acid starts with an acid head, the end with the red oxygens. On its own that head is a carboxyl group, COOH, and it reacts with one of glycerol's OH groups, giving off water, to make an ester link, the red bar that holds the fatty acid on.
segments.cue: Purple glycerol box, red oxygens and red ester bars

segments.name: Carbon Tails
segments.text: The long part sticking out to the right is the carbon tail, a zigzag of carbons numbered from the head, C1, out to the far end, which is called the omega end. There are only three elements here: carbon makes 4 bonds, oxygen makes 2 and hydrogen makes 1, and the hydrogens are hidden to keep the picture clean. In the tails, one line between carbons is a single bond, while the orange pair with two lines is a C=C double bond, and a double-bonded carbon has room for fewer hydrogens. The top chain has no double bonds, the middle one has one, and the bottom one has two.
segments.cue: Carbon tails and orange double bonds

segments.name: Straight and Saturated
segments.text: Here are the same 18 carbons three ways, and this time the small white hydrogens are shown. On top is stearic acid, which is saturated: there are no double bonds, so every tail carbon holds as many hydrogens as it can, two each and three on the end, and the zigzag runs straight. It melts at about 69 °C.

segments.name: The Cis Kink
segments.text: In the middle is oleic acid. Between C9 and C10 there's an orange double bond, and two hydrogens are gone, which is exactly what 'unsaturated' means. The two hydrogens left on that bond sit on the same side, which is called cis, and that bends the chain, so it melts at about 13 °C.
segments.cue: Middle row, orange C9=C10 and the kink

segments.name: Trans Stays Straight
segments.text: At the bottom is elaidic acid, a trans fat. It has the same double bond in the same place, but the hydrogens sit on opposite sides, so the chain stays nearly straight and melts at about 45 °C. So trans fat behaves much like saturated fat, while plant oils and most natural fats are cis.

segments.name: Where Trans Fat Comes From
segments.text: As the grey note says, most trans fat in food was man-made, by partial hydrogenation of vegetable oil, which we'll see in Figure 7. Small natural amounts come from ruminant animals, cows, sheep and goats, so dairy, beef and lamb contain a little, and the main one is vaccenic acid.

segments.name: Saturated Fat in Your Body
segments.text: In the pink box, saturated fat is part of the structure of your cell membranes and a dense backup fuel stored in fat tissue. Your liver can build cholesterol from fat breakdown products, and cholesterol is the raw material for steroid hormones, so the hormones come from cholesterol, not from saturated fat directly. But eating a lot of saturated fat raises LDL, the 'bad' cholesterol.

segments.name: Trans Fat in Your Body
segments.text: Trans fat is different: your body doesn't handle the straight trans shape like natural unsaturated fat, so it packs into cell membranes much like saturated fat. It raises LDL, the 'bad' cholesterol, lowers HDL, the 'good' one, and is strongly linked to heart disease, which is why industrial trans fat is now mostly banned in the US. Ruminant trans fat is eaten in much smaller amounts; at normal intakes the evidence of harm is weaker, but in high-dose trials it raises LDL too.
segments.cue: Pink box: Trans fat and Ruminant trans fat

segments.name: One Double Bond
segments.text: Unsaturated fats are grouped by how many double bonds they have. On top is oleic acid, which is monounsaturated, 'mono' meaning one: it has a single cis double bond at C9, and it's the main fat in olive oil.

segments.name: Two or More
segments.text: At the bottom is linoleic acid, which is polyunsaturated, 'poly' meaning many, with two cis double bonds at C9 and C12; it's in sunflower, corn and other seed oils. Each extra kink lowers the melting point again, from about 13 °C for oleic acid to about minus 5 °C for linoleic.

segments.name: Monounsaturated Fat in Your Body
segments.text: In the pink box, monounsaturated fat, mostly oleic acid, is the main fat in your stored body fat, your energy reserve, and it helps keep cell membranes flexible. Diets that swap saturated fat for monounsaturated fat are linked to better cholesterol numbers, with lower LDL and a better LDL-to-HDL balance.

segments.name: Essential Polyunsaturated Fats
segments.text: As for all polyunsaturated fats, the parent omega-3 and omega-6 are essential, so your body can't make them and they must come from food. Your body uses them to build signaling molecules called eicosanoids.

figures.title: Omega-3, omega-6 and omega-9

segments.name: Count From the Tail
segments.text: Now count from the tail end of the chain, where omega 1 is the last carbon. On top is ALA, the plant omega-3 in flax, chia and walnuts: it has three cis double bonds, and the first one starts at omega 3, so it's an omega-3.

segments.name: The Omega-6 Pattern
segments.text: Below it is linoleic acid, the main omega-6 in seed oils like sunflower and corn oil. It has two double bonds, and the first one starts at omega 6, so it's an omega-6.

segments.name: Omega-3 in Your Body
segments.text: In the pink box, omega-3 signals tend to calm inflammation, and DHA is a major building block of your brain and the retina of your eye. Plant ALA converts only poorly into EPA and DHA, so fish or algae are the direct sources.

segments.name: Omega-6 in Your Body
segments.text: Omega-6, through arachidonic acid, makes the signals for immune responses, inflammation and blood clotting, and those are useful jobs. But too much omega-6 compared with omega-3 may tip the balance toward inflammation.

segments.name: Two Ends
segments.text: A fatty acid has two ends. The acid end, the COOH group, is carbon 1, and it's the end that joins glycerol. The other end is a CH3 group called the omega end. Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, so it just means the far end.
segments.cue: Lower diagram: acid end on the left, omega end on the right

segments.name: Omega Is an Address
segments.text: An omega number is an address. Omega-3, omega-6 and omega-9 tell you the first double bond starts 3, 6 or 9 carbons in from the omega end. The grey omega numbers count that way; the blue numbers count from the acid end.
segments.cue: Grey ω numbers vs blue carbon numbers

segments.name: Desaturases Add Double Bonds
segments.text: Your body makes double bonds with enzymes called desaturases. A desaturase takes two hydrogens off a chain and turns a single carbon-carbon bond into a double bond, and each one works at a fixed spot, counted from the acid end.

segments.name: How Far Human Enzymes Reach
segments.text: Human desaturases only reach the first nine carbons from the acid end; that is called delta 9. That is enough to put a double bond at carbon 9 and turn stearic acid into oleic acid. On an eighteen-carbon chain carbon 9 is also omega 9, so omega-9 is not essential: your body makes it.
segments.cue: Top row: oleic acid, ring inside the blue zone

segments.name: Out of Reach: Carbons 12 and 15
segments.text: On the same eighteen-carbon chain, the omega-6 double bond sits at carbon 12 and the omega-3 double bond at carbon 15. Humans lack the delta 12 and delta 15 desaturases that put them there. Plants, algae and some microbes have them.
segments.cue: Middle and bottom rows: dashed rings in the green zone

segments.name: Why LA and ALA Are Essential
segments.text: That's why linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are the essential fatty acids: you have to eat them. Animals and fish don't make them either; they get them from plants and algae.

segments.name: Building Longer Chains
segments.text: Your body can lengthen these chains and add more double bonds near the acid end. Linoleic acid becomes arachidonic acid, and ALA becomes EPA and then DHA. But only a small share of ALA gets that far, so fish and algae, which supply EPA and DHA ready-made, matter.

segments.name: No Switching Families
segments.text: The omega end is never changed. So an omega-6 stays an omega-6 and an omega-3 stays an omega-3; your body can't turn one into the other, and you need both.

segments.name: The Rule of Thumb
segments.text: So the rule of thumb is: your body can edit a chain near the acid end, but not near the omega end.

figures.subtitle: Counted from the tail end; only omega-9 can be made by your body.

figures.title: Hydrogenation: how oils become solid fats

segments.name: Adding Hydrogen
segments.text: This is how factories turn liquid oil into solid fat: starting from the oil at the top, they add hydrogen gas with a nickel catalyst and heat.

segments.name: Full Versus Partial
segments.text: Full hydrogenation, at the bottom, removes every double bond and gives saturated fat. Partial hydrogenation, in the middle, stops partway, so some double bonds remain and some flip from cis to trans.

segments.name: Where Trans Fat Came From
segments.text: That's where most trans fat in food came from, the man-made trans fat from Figure 4. Industrial trans fat is now banned in the US and limited in the EU.

segments.name: Melting Points
segments.text: At the top are the melting points of the pure fatty acids, and the dashed line is room temperature. Anything above it, like stearic and elaidic acid, is solid in your kitchen, and anything below, like oleic, linoleic and ALA, is liquid.

segments.name: What Sets the Melting Point
segments.text: The pattern is simple: straighter chains melt higher, every cis kink lowers the melting point, and longer chains melt higher.

segments.name: Fat Inside You
segments.text: At the bottom is the same idea inside you. Stored body fat is mostly triglycerides, and most of their fatty acids are unsaturated, with oleic acid the most common, so it stays soft at body temperature, about 37 °C. Fat just under the cooler skin is firmer, and fat deeper in is softer.

segments.name: An Evidence Note
segments.text: You'll sometimes hear that the body keeps its outer fat layers more unsaturated so they don't harden. That's well shown in pigs and other animals, but the evidence in humans is weaker, so treat it as a maybe.

segments.name: Back to the Family Tree
segments.text: That completes the family tree from Figure 1: saturated, mono with omega-9, poly with omega-3 and omega-6, and trans. Next, Figure 9 shows how your body breaks a fat down for energy.
segments.cue: Back to Figure 1 if there is time

figures.title: Breaking a fat down for energy

segments.name: Many Kinds of Triglyceride
segments.text: Not every triglyceride is the same. The glycerol backbone has three slots, and each slot can hold a different fatty acid: saturated or unsaturated, short or long, omega-3 or omega-6. Which chains sit in which slots is what makes one specific triglyceride different from another. With about twenty common fatty acids in food, that's already around eight thousand possible combinations, because twenty times twenty times twenty is eight thousand and the order of the slots matters, so in practice there are thousands of different triglycerides, and every food fat is a mix of many of them. Olive oil, for example, is mostly triglycerides with oleic acid in two or three of the slots, while butter mixes short, medium and long saturated chains.
segments.cue: Panel A: tristearin S-S-S, triolein O-O-O, the mixed P-O-L one; slots 1, 2, 3

segments.name: Breakdown and Release
segments.text: When your body is low on energy, for example between meals, during exercise or overnight, hormones like adrenaline and glucagon rise and insulin falls, and that switches on the fat-releasing enzymes in your fat tissue: adipose triglyceride lipase starts the job and hormone-sensitive lipase continues it. Together they snip a triglyceride apart into its pieces: one glycerol plus three free fatty acids. The cut happens at the ester links, where each fatty acid's carboxyl end, the part with the oxygens, was attached to the glycerol backbone; water is added at each link, so the acid head is restored. The glycerol is small and water-soluble, so it travels to the liver, which can turn it into glucose. The fatty acids don't dissolve well in blood, so they ride on a carrier protein called albumin to muscle and the heart, where they're burned for fuel. In a deeper or longer fast, the liver takes up more of them and turns part of them into ketones, a backup fuel even the brain can use. Inside the cell, the chain is chopped two carbons at a time, a process called beta-oxidation. The oxygen end is just the handle; the real energy payoff is in the long run of carbon-hydrogen bonds, which is why fat gives 9 calories per gram.
segments.cue: Panel B, left to right: the 3 cuts (+ H2O), glycerol and 3 fatty acids, then liver and muscle/heart; after this, Figure 10 recaps the module

figures.title: Putting It All Together
figures.subtitle: A recap of the whole module.

segments.name: The Whole Family
segments.text: That's the whole module, so Figure 10 puts it all together. This is the family tree from Figure 1 again, but now every branch has its molecule next to it, all drawn at the same scale with every hydrogen showing. At the top is the triglyceride, the form almost all fat takes in food and in your body: a glycerol backbone holding three fatty acids by ester links. This one carries palmitic, oleic and linoleic acid, which is typical, because every food fat is a mix. Everything below it is about those fatty-acid chains, and what sorts them into families is the double bonds between carbons: how many there are, where they sit, and which way the hydrogens point around them.
segments.cue: Top node: the triglyceride, glycerol in the purple box, ester links in red; then follow the lines down

segments.name: Saturated
segments.text: Saturated fat has no double bonds at all. Every carbon in the tail holds as many hydrogens as it can, so the zigzag runs straight, the chains pack tightly, and the fat is solid at room temperature. Our example is stearic acid, eighteen carbons, which melts at about sixty-nine degrees Celsius. You find saturated fat in butter, cheese, beef and lamb fat, coconut and cocoa butter. Mainstream guidelines suggest keeping it under about ten percent of daily calories, because eating a lot of it raises LDL cholesterol.
segments.cue: Left branch: Saturated, the straight stearic chain, then the e.g. line

segments.name: Unsaturated
segments.text: Unsaturated fats have at least one carbon-carbon double bond, and in food these are almost always cis, so each one puts a kink in the chain and the fat usually stays liquid. Monounsaturated means exactly one, and most of it is omega-9: oleic acid, the main fat in olive oil, avocados, almonds and macadamias. Your body makes oleic acid itself, so omega-9 isn't essential. Polyunsaturated means two or more, and that's where omega-3 and omega-6 come in, named by counting from the tail end. Alpha-linolenic acid, ALA, has its first double bond three carbons from the end, so it's an omega-3, from flax, chia and walnuts. Linoleic acid starts at the sixth carbon from the end, so it's an omega-6, from seeds, nuts and poultry. Those two are the essential fatty acids: your body can't make them, so they have to come from food. Your body can turn some ALA into EPA and DHA, but only a small fraction, so oily fish and algae are the direct sources.
segments.cue: Middle branch: Monounsaturated → Omega-9 (oleic), and Polyunsaturated → Omega-3 (ALA) and Omega-6 (linoleic); tap a molecule to enlarge it

segments.name: Trans
segments.text: Trans fat has the same kind of double bond as oleic acid, but its hydrogens sit on opposite sides, so the chain stays nearly straight and behaves like saturated fat. Elaidic acid is the classic example. Most trans fat in food was made by partially hydrogenating unsaturated oils, the dashed arrow in Figure 1, and small natural amounts come from dairy, beef and lamb. It raises LDL and lowers HDL, which is why industrial trans fat is now banned in the US.
segments.cue: Right branch: Trans, the nearly straight elaidic chain; compare with oleic, bottom left

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few extras worth knowing. Fat gives about nine calories per gram, against about four for carbohydrate and protein and about seven for alcohol. Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat, so you absorb them along with the fat in a meal. Cholesterol is also a lipid, but it isn't a triglyceride at all: it's a sterol, built from four fused carbon rings. Your liver makes most of what you need, and in food it comes only from animal products. LDL and HDL aren't two kinds of cholesterol; they're the particles that carry it in the blood. And no food fat is just one type: olive oil is about three-quarters monounsaturated and butter about two-thirds saturated. The table sums up the fat types side by side. This is general education, not medical advice, and the quiz is right below.
segments.cue: Worth knowing: energy per gram, the comparison table, essential fatty acids, vitamins, cholesterol

segments.name: Lipids in the Body
segments.text: Lipids in the human body, by share of total body lipid. Reference adult: about 70 kilograms, with about 13.5 kilograms of lipid in all, most of it in about 15 kilograms of fat tissue. Triglycerides, about 95 percent, about 12.8 kilograms: stored fat, almost all of it in fat tissue, about 12 kilograms, with smaller stores in muscle, liver, bone marrow and blood. Phospholipids, about 4 percent, about half a kilogram: the double layer of every cell membrane, most of it in muscle, brain and liver. Cholesterol, about 1 percent, about 150 grams: mostly free cholesterol in cell membranes, about a quarter of it in the brain and nerves, plus some stored as cholesterol esters. Miscellaneous, each under 1 percent, under half a percent together, about 50 grams: glycolipids, mostly in the brain, free fatty acids, the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, coenzyme Q10, carotenoids, bile acids, steroid hormones, eicosanoids, and skin waxes and ceramides.
